chapters.title: Part IA: Time Value of Money
chapters.description: Valuation principle, timelines, compounding, discounting and present value.

questions.stem: Why is a euro received today generally worth more than a euro received one year from today, assuming a positive interest rate?

options.text: A euro received today can be invested to earn a return.
A euro received in the future cannot be spent.
Inflation must always be zero today.
Future cash flows have no financial value.

questions.explanation: Money received today can be invested and earn a return before the later date. This is the basic time value of money.
questions.source: Part 1A, 3.3 The Time Value of Money; sample test Q1

questions.stem: On a standard cash-flow timeline, what does date 0 represent?

options.text: The end of the first year.
The beginning of the second year.
Today, the beginning of the first period.
The date on which the final cash flow is received.

questions.explanation: Date 0 is today. Date 1 is the end of the first period, date 2 the end of the second, and so on.

questions.stem: You deposit €1,500 today in an account paying 4% interest per year, compounded annually. How much will be in the account after two years?
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 2: Compounding; sample test Q3

questions.stem: What is the present value of €2,420 to be received in two years if the annual discount rate is 10%?
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 3: Discounting; sample test Q4

questions.stem: Two investments have the same total amount of positive cash flows, but one pays more of its cash flows earlier. With a positive discount rate, which statement is generally correct?

options.text: The investments must have the same present value.
The investment with earlier cash flows generally has the higher present value.
The investment with later cash flows always has the higher present value.
Timing does not affect present value.

questions.explanation: Earlier cash flows are discounted for fewer periods, so with a positive discount rate they generally have a higher present value, all else equal.
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 3: Discounting; sample test Q5

questions.stem: Which statement best describes compound interest?

options.text: Interest is calculated only on the original amount in every period.
The interest rate must increase each year.
Interest is earned on the original amount and on interest already accumulated.
It applies only when an investment lasts for one year.

questions.explanation: Under compound interest, previously accumulated interest also earns interest in later periods ('interest on interest').
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 2: Compound Interest; sample test Q6

questions.stem: In a standard present-value calculation, the discount rate is most closely related to:

options.text: The number of cash flows in the investment.
The accounting profit reported last year.
The face value of the future cash flow.
The return available on an investment of comparable risk.

questions.explanation: The discount rate reflects the return available on comparable-risk investments and converts future cash flows into present-value terms.
questions.source: Part 1A, Discount Factors and Rates; sample test Q7

questions.stem: Why must cash flows occurring at different dates be converted to the same point in time before they are compared or added?

options.text: Cash flows at different dates must always be negative.
Interest rates can be applied only to the first cash flow.
Every cash flow must be converted to a future value, never a present value.
Amounts at different dates are not directly comparable because of the time value of money.

questions.explanation: A euro today and a euro received later are not equivalent. Cash flows must be compounded or discounted to a common date first (Rule 1).
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 1: Comparing and Combining Values; sample test Q10

questions.stem: All else equal, what happens to the present value of a fixed positive cash flow when the discount rate increases?

options.text: It increases.
It decreases.
It remains unchanged.
It becomes equal to the future value.

questions.explanation: PV = C/(1 + r)^n. A higher discount rate increases the denominator, which reduces the present value of a positive future cash flow.
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 3: Discounting; sample test Q11

questions.stem: A company invests €2,500 today at 8% interest compounded annually. What is the future value after three years?
questions.source: Part 1A, Rule 2: Compounding; sample test Q12

chapters.title: Part IB: Cash-Flow Valuation
chapters.description: Streams of cash flows, annuities, perpetuities and growing cash flows.

questions.stem: A project pays €1,000 at the end of Year 1 and €1,000 at the end of Year 2. If the annual discount rate is 10%, what is the present value of the two payments?
questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow separately and add: €1,000/1.10 + €1,000/1.10^2 = €909.09 + €826.45 = €1,735.54.
questions.source: Part 1B, 4.1 Valuing a Stream of Cash Flows; sample test Q8

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes an ordinary annuity?

options.text: Equal payments made at the end of each period for a finite number of periods.
Equal payments made forever, with no final payment.
One payment made immediately.
Payments that must increase by the same percentage every period.

questions.explanation: An ordinary annuity is equal payments at regular intervals, made at the end of each period, for a fixed number of periods.

questions.stem: What is the present value of an ordinary annuity paying €300 at the end of each year for four years, if the annual discount rate is 10%?
questions.source: Part 1B, Present Value of an Annuity; sample test Q13

questions.stem: A level perpetuity pays €400 at the end of every year, with the first payment one year from today. If the annual discount rate is 8%, what is its present value?
questions.explanation: For a level perpetuity with the first payment one period from now, PV = C/r = €400 / 0.08 = €5,000.

questions.stem: A growing perpetuity has a next-period cash flow of €600, a discount rate of 10%, and a constant growth rate of 4%. Assuming the rate exceeds the growth rate, what is its present value?
questions.explanation: PV = C1/(r − g) = €600 / (0.10 − 0.04) = €10,000. The formula requires r > g.
questions.source: Part 1B, 4.4 Growing Cash Flows; sample test Q15
